accroche: An iron bar passes through his skull in 1848. What the medical record documents is narrower, and more interesting, than the legend.
contenu_vulgarise:
On September 13, 1848, near Cavendish, Vermont, an accidental explosion sends a tamping iron one meter long through the face and then the skull of Phineas Gage, foreman of a blasting crew. He remains conscious. He speaks almost immediately after the accident.

## A Surprisingly Thin Medical Record

The physician John Martyn Harlow treats him and publishes a first report as early as 1848, centered on the physical aspects of the wound. He states explicitly that he is reserving the analysis of Gage's behavior for a future paper. It is not until 1868, twenty years later, drawing on his correspondence with the family, that Harlow publishes the text that will found the whole legend: a few sentences, and nothing more, on a change of character.

This text, which can now be read online, sets neither a chronology nor a duration. Yet it is on these few lines that, for more than a century, the image will rest of a Gage who became coarse, unable to hold a job, methodically destroyed by his injury.

## What Gage Did Next

The documented facts tell a different story. In 1852, Gage goes to Chile to set up a stagecoach line in Valparaíso. He stays there nearly eight years, looking after horses and himself driving heavily loaded coaches, skilled work, incompatible with the image of a man permanently out of control. He returns to the United States, weakened by epileptic seizures, only shortly before his death.

The historian of neuroscience Malcolm Macmillan, who devoted an entire book to reconstructing this record, even corrected an error by Harlow himself: the date of Gage's death, which Harlow placed in 1861, must in fact be moved up to 1860, according to burial records. If the only primary source on the case contains a date error that went unnoticed for a century, what are we to make of everything the legend has added to it with no source at all?

In 2009, the rediscovery of a daguerreotype showing Gage holding his iron bar completed the cracking of the received image: it shows a well-groomed, well-dressed man, with a composed air, a world away from the disheveled and menacing figure that oral tradition had ended up drawing.

## What This Shifts

The Gage case has remained a pillar of neuropsychology because it shows, better than any other example, how fast a thin medical fact can turn into popular certainty, each retelling adding a detail that no source contains. The lesson holds today for any scientific anecdote that circulates without anyone having reopened the original file.

carte.punch: Phineas Gage's real medical record fits in a few sentences, not in a legend.
carte.idee: In 1848, an iron bar passes through Phineas Gage's skull. The only text on his change of character, written twenty years later, amounts to a few vague sentences. Gage then worked for several years as a coachman in Chile, far from the permanently destroyed man the legend built.

quiz.question: What does Harlow's record, the only primary source on Gage's change in behavior, really say?
choix: Nothing: Harlow never mentioned a change of personality
A real change, but described in a few vague sentences, with no duration specified
An immediate shift to violence, documented over several years
A complete clinical diagnosis including memory and language tests
quiz.explication: The 1868 text, written twenty years after the accident, devotes only a few imprecise sentences to the change in behavior, with no chronology or duration. Later versions, violence, social decline, amplified this short passage far beyond what Harlow actually wrote, whereas Gage then worked for several years as a coachman in Chile.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Phineas Gage do after his accident, between 1852 and about 1860?
choix: He remained hospitalized under constant observation in Vermont
He went to Chile to run a stagecoach line, looking after horses for nearly eight years
He began a traveling fairground tour across the United States
He went back to his post as foreman of a blasting crew in Vermont
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Gage goes to Chile in 1852 to set up a stagecoach line in Valparaíso, where he stays nearly eight years looking after horses and driving heavily loaded coaches.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What error did Malcolm Macmillan correct in Harlow's own record?
choix: The date of the accident, which he moved up from 1848 to 1847
The place of the accident, actually located in New Hampshire
The date of Gage's death, to be corrected from 1861 to 1860 according to burial records
Gage's first name, wrongly spelled “Phinehas” by Harlow
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Macmillan corrected an error by Harlow himself: the date of Gage's death, which Harlow placed in 1861, must be moved up to 1860 according to burial records.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the rediscovery of a daguerreotype of Gage in 2009 reveal?
choix: A well-groomed, well-dressed man with a composed air, holding the iron bar
That Gage in fact wore a permanent bandage on his face
That Gage had lost an eye in the accident, contrary to what was thought
That the iron bar displayed in museums was not the right one
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 2009 daguerreotype shows a well-groomed, well-dressed man with a composed air, a world away from the disheveled and menacing figure that oral tradition had ended up drawing.
